anchor: uncover significant, previously unknown bugs in \emph{both} comprehensive defenses that we test---STT and SPT.
comment: Overclaim that contradicts the intro and the repo. The intro reports one new bug (a visibility-point/squash race shared by STT and SPT). The results doc calls the SPT case the same shared logic with no independent SPT bug, still open (A5), and says the race shows up only under modified timing (0 hits at stock timing). A reviewer will read 'bugs in both' as two independent bugs.
proposed: Say 'uncover a previously unknown visibility-point/squash timing race shared by STT and SPT', and state that it appears under stressed timing.

anchor: found that only 15\% percent of AMuLeT's randomly synthesized tests even contain the basic components necessary for leakage.
comment: This number is wrong and contradicts the paper's own results: results.tex:134 and the repo both give 17% (85 of 500 AMuLeT STT tests contain a window-valid transmitter gadget). The 15% in the abstract is a different metric (test count needed to reach a bug), so the two statements also conflict with each other.
proposed: Change it to 17% (85/500 window-valid gadgets), and drop the duplicated 'percent'.

anchor: we show that our test generation corpus takes 15\% of the test count of prior work to rediscover known bugs.
comment: This generalizes from one data point. The repo's efficiency measurement covers a single bug on a single build (SpecLFB UV6: first hit at test #6 vs. AMuLeT's #39, about 15%), yet the sentence says 'known bugs' in the plural. Readers will also confuse it with the intro's '15% of AMuLeT tests contain leakage components', which is a different claim.
proposed: Something like: 'on SpecLFB, SimSpect reaches the known first-load bug in 6.5x fewer tests than AMuLeT', and keep the gadget-fraction (17%) claim separate.

anchor: SPO, SPT, and ReCon \anna{invisispec, lfb, cleanup}; and can therefore generate comprehensive litmus test suites up to specified bounds for each test.
comment: Overclaim that the repo doesn't support. STAGE1_alloy/models has defense models only for STT, SPT and Recon (no SpecShield, NDA, DoM or SPO model). The paper's own Discussion says SpecLFB, InvisiSpec and CleanupSpec reuse STT's model. 'SPO' also appears nowhere else in the repo, and related.tex writes it as 'SPO/SPT'.
proposed: List only the defenses that have models and test suites (STT, SPT, Recon, plus the ones that reuse the STT model), or call the others 'expressible' rather than 'expressed'.

anchor: The test sets generated by \toolname are complete in including all fundamental leakage path skeletons, and are diversified across timing, instruction type, and speculation direction.
comment: This completeness claim (also in 'capturing all leakage scenarios' and 'target all possible types of violations ... providing assurance of design correctness') contradicts the Discussion, which says the suite is complete only up to the bound once Stage 1 reaches UNSAT and that Stage 1.5 is non-exhaustive. Also, the real testsets are capped at max_instances (100k), so the cap left out shapes such as the OTB gadget. Reviewers will attack an unqualified 'all'.
proposed: Qualify it: 'complete up to the instruction bound (when enumeration reaches UNSAT)', and drop 'assurance of design correctness'.

anchor: instrument a simulator to execute with said speculation annotations, inducing potential violations.
comment: Garbled text: this is a dangling sentence fragment left over from an edit. The same paragraph also says SimSpect validates 'against a security contract', which is the term the previous paragraph uses for AMuLeT's higher-level property. That blurs the paper's main distinction (defense's own guarantee vs. a generic contract). The \anna marker will be hidden, but this text will still render.
proposed: Merge it into the previous sentence ('...a harness that instruments the simulator to follow these speculation annotations, inducing the modeled violations'), and use 'defense security guarantee' rather than 'security contract' for SimSpect.

anchor: We therefore consider the class of defenses with some hardware component \cite{?}.
comment: Broken citations will render as [?] in the PDF the lab sees: \cite{?} here, and the keys nickscommittoSTT (intro), NDA (background; the bib key is lowercase 'nda'), yaos-micro-paper and alloy (background) are all missing from references.bib. Citing an STT bug with [?] is especially bad.
proposed: Fix the keys (NDA->nda), add the missing bib entries, or remove the citations.
evidence: references.bib (no keys: NDA, nickscommittoSTT, yaos-micro-paper, alloy)

anchor: is another defense that stalls earlier in the violating path, before an instruction can load a secret piece of data \cite{NDA}.
comment: Likely mischaracterization of NDA (from memory, unverified against the NDA paper): NDA lets the speculative load access data and blocks propagation of the loaded value to dependent instructions. It does not stop the load itself. The lab knows NDA well.
proposed: Something like: 'NDA blocks speculatively loaded data from propagating to dependent instructions until the load is safe.' Check the wording against the NDA paper.
evidence: from memory, unverified (NDA, Weisse et al.); bib key is 'nda'

anchor: when supplied with two different inputs, are indistinguishable in their architectural side-channel leakage.
comment: This garbles relational testing. AMuLeT runs input pairs that the contract says are indistinguishable and checks whether the microarchitectural traces differ; the inputs are not 'indistinguishable in their architectural side-channel leakage'. It also disagrees with the intro's description ('two randomly generated architecturally identical tests'). Nearby, 'analyzes fabricated designs or RTL, due to the wide availability' is not a coherent sentence.
proposed: Something like: 'runs pairs of inputs that are equivalent under a security contract and flags differences in observed microarchitectural state.'

anchor: there exists no comprehensive early-stage validation method for their proposed security guarantees.
comment: Earlier in this sentence the abstract says the bugs 'invalidate their performance guarantees'. That reverses the argument: security bugs invalidate the prototypes' performance results (overhead estimates), as the intro argues. Defenses don't come with performance guarantees. The abstract's other claim, that SimSpect 'prov[es] security properties', also overreaches, since the intro presents the work as validation, not proof.
proposed: Use 'invalidate their reported performance results', and change 'proving security properties' to 'reasoning about security properties' unless a proof appears in the paper.
